claims.text: Brief low-temperature annealing immediately after ultra-rapid solidification will relax quenched-in internal stresses.
The post-quench annealing treatment will improve short-range atomic ordering.
Post-quench annealing will enhance glass-forming ability relative to rapid quenching alone.
Post-quench annealing will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state relative to rapid quenching alone.
Ultra-rapid cooling such as melt-spinning can produce a predominantly amorphous phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy.
Annealing a few tens of kelvin below the glass-transition temperature is an appropriate implementation of the intervention.
The annealing temperature must remain below the crystallization onset.
An inert atmosphere is required for the beneficial annealing treatment.
Annealing below the crystallization onset permits stress relaxation without significant atomic diffusion.
An annealing duration on the order of a few minutes can provide sufficient relaxation without inducing crystallization.
The intervention will enhance medium-range atomic ordering without forming crystalline nuclei.
Low-temperature annealing facilitates atomic rearrangements that relieve residual stresses trapped during ultrafast quenching.
Relieving residual stresses lowers the driving force for undesired heterogeneous nucleation.
Stress relief raises the effective energy barrier for crystallization.
The annealed sample will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than the unannealed control.
The annealed sample will retain a more robust amorphous structure detectable by XRD and TEM.
A higher crystallization-onset temperature and improved amorphous retention indicate enhanced glass-forming ability as well as enhanced thermal stability.
Annealing for too long or at too high a temperature may cause crystallization and negate the improvement in glass stability.

contradictions.description: The intervention is applied only after the glass has already been formed, yet the hypothesis claims improved glass-forming ability. The proposed measurements assess subsequent crystallization resistance and amorphous retention, not the ability to form glass during quenching, such as critical cooling rate or critical casting thickness.
